title: Generation 1 — roughly the 1440s–1540s
description:
Kumaon at this time was divided among local rulers, with the Chand kings steadily extending their rule from Champawat across the hills. The area around present-day Chaukhutia and Dwarahat had long been part of the older Katyuri world, whose temples still stand there.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 2 — roughly the 1470s–1570s
description:
The Chand kings were consolidating their hold over Kumaon. Around the 1560s they moved their capital from Champawat to Almora — the beginning of Almora's centuries as the region's political centre.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 3 — roughly the 1500s–1590s
description:
Kumaon under Chand rule from Almora. Village life across the hills was built on terraced farming, livestock, and seasonal movement between higher and lower pastures.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 4 — roughly the 1530s–1620s
description:
Continued Chand rule. The Ramganga valley, where Chaukhutia sits, was a natural route between Kumaon and Garhwal — trade and travel between the two passed through valleys like it.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 5 — roughly the 1560s–1640s
description:
A long, relatively settled stretch of Chand rule over Kumaon, marked by temple patronage and the growth of Almora as a town.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 6 — roughly the 1590s–1670s
description:
Chand-era Kumaon. Repeated conflicts with the neighbouring kingdom of Garhwal shaped the western borderlands — the direction in which the Ramganga valley opens.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 7 — roughly the 1620s–1690s
description:
Chand rule continued from Almora, with the hill villages largely self-sufficient: grain, pulses, and milk from their own fields and cattle.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 8 — roughly the 1650s–1720s
description:
In the 1740s, Rohilla forces from the plains invaded and plundered Almora — one of the most destructive events in the Chand kingdom's history.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 9 — roughly the 1680s–1740s
description:
The Chand kingdom was weakening, with power struggles among ministers and court families in Almora.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 10 — roughly the 1710s–1770s
description:
The end of the Chand era. In 1790 the Gorkhas of Nepal conquered Kumaon.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 11 — roughly the 1740s–1790s
description:
Kumaon under Gorkha administration (1790–1815), a period remembered in Kumaoni oral tradition as harsh, with heavy taxes and forced labour.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 12 — roughly the 1770s–1820s
description:
After the Anglo-Nepalese War, Kumaon came under the British East India Company in 1815. New land settlements and revenue records began to be made for villages across the hills.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 13 — roughly the 1800s–1840s
description:
Early British Kumaon. Roads, forest rules, and district administration gradually reached the interior valleys.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 14 — roughly the 1830s–1870s
description:
The decades around the 1857 uprising, and the transfer of India from the Company to the British Crown. Hill stations like Ranikhet were founded nearby soon after.

(Dates are estimated backward from generation 19, at roughly 25–30 years per generation. The further back, the wider the uncertainty.)

title: Generation 15 — roughly the 1860s–1890s
description:
Late 19th / early 20th-century British Kumaon.

The house believed to have been built in this generation is the last known residence of the Pandey clan that still stands today. It was shared by {{children:laxmidutt}}, and was presumably built by Laxmi Dutt.

title: Generation 16 — roughly the 1890s–1920s
description: Early 20th century. In 1921, at the Uttarayani fair in Bageshwar, Kumaonis publicly ended the forced-labour 'coolie begar' system — a landmark protest in the region's history. Many Kumaoni men also served in the World Wars.

title: Generation 17 — roughly the 1920s–1940s
description: The freedom movement reached deep into the hills; during the 1942 Quit India movement there were major protests across Almora district.

title: Generation 18 — roughly the 1950s–1970s
description: Independent India. Kumaon was part of Uttar Pradesh, and migration from the hills to the plains for education and work became common.

title: Generation 19 — roughly 1983–1995
description: The years of the Uttarakhand statehood movement, which culminated in the new state being formed in 2000.

title: Generation 20 — recent years
description: The newest generation recorded in this tree.
